projects.title: Mode/s of Making
projects.subtitle: Heat rotate cutting
projects.summary: A studio investigation into how machine motion, cutting paths and material texture can shape the design of custom polystyrene units.
projects.metadataDescription: A source-backed studio study connecting rotary heat cutting, custom polystyrene units, machine design and physical surface prototypes.
projects.context: National Cheng Kung University · Tainan, Taiwan
projects.role: Studio design, toolpath development and fabrication research

hero.alt: Digital visualization of curved polystyrene units assembled into a repeating wall.
hero.caption: Simulation detail of the proposed custom-unit assembly.
hero.credit: Design study: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Design begins with the tool.
paragraphs: Mode/s of Making investigates the machine as a design tool. The study connects the geometry of polystyrene units with the motion of a rotary heat-cutting prototype.
The proposed assemblies develop from individual curved units. Digital studies explore how those units meet and how changes in cutting profiles affect the larger pattern.

media.alt: The complete landscape visualization joins curved-unit assemblies, a rotary cutting setup and its exploded machine components.
media.caption: Imagined fabrication and assembly, with the cutting machine’s exploded components.
media.credit: Design study: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: System
sections.title: From geometry to coordinated motion.
paragraphs: The recorded workflow links geometry development, cutting-path optimisation, G-code conversion, machine setup and assembly guided by the simulation model.
The system combines a CoreXY mechanism for planar movement with a stepper-controlled rotary holder. Arduino and Marlin provide existing control infrastructure for the design-to-fabrication workflow.

media.alt: Diagram linking geometry and cutting profiles to G-code, a controller and the rotary cutting machine.
media.caption: The original workflow from geometry development to fabrication and assembly.
media.credit: Design study: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

media.alt: Machine diagram showing CoreXY movement, the rotary holder, endstop and controller.
media.caption: Planar tool motion and a rotating holder form the machine system.
media.credit: Design study: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Building a fabrication prototype.
paragraphs: The prototype uses an aluminium frame, 3D-printed components and a holder that accommodates different material sizes. The rotating axis controls section position while planar movement follows the cutting profile.
The exploded model describes the relationships between motors, rods, belts, bearings and the cutting tool. The workshop photograph records an assembled prototype with a polystyrene blank.

media.alt: The complete landscape visualization joins curved-unit assemblies, a rotary cutting setup and its exploded machine components.
media.caption: Imagined fabrication and assembly, with the cutting machine’s exploded components.
media.credit: Design study: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

media.alt: An aluminium-frame cutting machine holds a cylindrical polystyrene blank.
media.caption: An original studio fabrication record of the rotary cutting prototype.
media.credit: Studio fabrication record. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Toolpaths become surface texture.
paragraphs: The portfolio describes a roughing stage followed by a slower continuous finishing pass. The physical studies show how the path leaves a texture across the cut surface.
Those material traces feed back into the design investigation. Physical prototypes document joints and surface details, while the larger assemblies remain identified as digital visualisations.

media.alt: Physical polystyrene prototypes show assembled joints and layered cutting textures.
media.caption: Physical prototypes and the textures left by the cutting process.
media.credit: Jan Kyselý (Figs. 5-09 and 5-10); other photographs not individually credited.

projects.title: Entrance Installation Art
projects.subtitle: Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square
projects.summary: Translating a patterned surface into folded metal panels, connection details and fabrication drawings for an entrance installation.
projects.metadataDescription: Scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication-drawing coordination for the Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square entrance installation.
projects.role: Scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication drawings

hero.alt: View upward along the completed installation, with folded triangular metal panels and openings.
hero.caption: The folded panel surface of the Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square entrance installation.
hero.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A surface becomes a panel system.
paragraphs: The installation begins with a NURBS surface. Triangular subdivision responds to fabrication constraints, and controlled panel depth gives the surface its relief.
A helical curve provides a distance relationship for varying the openings. The project develops several pattern schemes within the same overall geometry.

media.alt: Four digital models progress from a smooth surface to triangulation, depth and openings.
media.caption: Surface subdivision, panel depth and a helical distance field develop the pattern.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

media.alt: A grid of related installation models compares different panel opening patterns.
media.caption: Pattern schemes developed within the same overall installation geometry.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Connections organise the surface.
paragraphs: The documented system uses two-ear and three-ear folded panels supported by module hangers. Each panel edge and connection responds to the required local depth.
Paired fixing and alignment holes coordinate neighbouring panels. The section and joint studies connect the outer pattern with its internal support system.

media.alt: Section and joint illustrations show the support frame and two-ear and three-ear folded panels.
media.caption: The support system and the two families of folded panel connections.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Turning model data into drawings.
paragraphs: The work translates 3D geometry into flat fabrication information: cutting and folding lines, hole positions, panel dimensions and folding angles.
The drawings combine model-derived information with manual checks for delivery to the local fabrication team. Workshop photographs record the supports and modules during production.

media.alt: Flat panel drawings retain fold lines, holes, dimensions and folding-angle information.
media.caption: The model is translated into dimensioned fabrication drawings for individual panels.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

media.alt: Workshop photographs show internal supports and the installation modules during fabrication.
media.caption: Workshop documentation of the internal supports and separately fabricated modules.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Reading the assembled geometry.
paragraphs: The completed surface retains the variation of individual openings while forming a continuous entrance installation. Close views reveal folds, edges and the relationship between neighbouring panels.
My documented role covers scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication drawings within the engineering team. The 2D and structural sectors are credited separately below.

media.alt: Photographs show the completed installation, close panel details and its urban setting.
media.caption: Built surface details and the entrance installation in its site context.
media.credit: Project documentation: PKD Engineering Consultants. Individual image author not separately identified.

projects.title: Dot-Based 3D Printing
projects.subtitle: Printing Architecture · Dot-based non-planar fabrication
projects.summary: A collaborative study of how layer height, density, speed and path delays produce surface patterns across different printed geometries.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team project exploring dot-based non-planar printing through parameter samples, deposition strategies and physical prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland

hero.alt: A translucent twisted printed object stands in snow against grass and trees.
hero.caption: A physical prototype from the dot-based non-planar printing study.
hero.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Parameters become material patterns.
paragraphs: The study begins with printed samples that vary layer height, density, printing speed and pattern settings. Their surfaces provide a physical record of how those choices affect bead spacing and texture.
The same investigation extends from small samples to more complex forms, carrying the dotted surface language into curved and twisted geometries.

media.alt: A parameter diagram and twelve printed samples compare dotted and continuous textures.
media.caption: Layer height, density, pattern and speed are explored through a family of printed samples.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Coordinating paths and delays.
paragraphs: The documented strategies vary the robotic path and introduce time delays during deposition. Smooth and dotted regions emerge through different combinations of movement and material placement.
Path diagrams sit beside printed samples so that the relationship between motion strategy and surface formation can be read directly.

media.alt: Three path diagrams are paired with printed rings and close views of deposited beads.
media.caption: Different deposition paths and time-delay strategies produce different bead patterns.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

media.alt: Three printed shapes are paired with digital line models of their increasingly twisted geometries.
media.caption: The printing strategy is explored across a sequence of different overall forms.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Observing the deposition process.
paragraphs: The fabrication record shows material deposited along the specimen edge by the printing nozzle. A still from the original Group1 recording preserves this stage of the process.
The project is documented as team research. The available sources confirm participation but do not separately allocate every slicer, robot-operation or photography task.

media.alt: A printing nozzle deposits material along the upper edge of a dotted specimen.
media.caption: A still frame from the original Group1 fabrication recording.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: A family of physical experiments.
paragraphs: The geometry-development prototypes explore different overall twists while retaining visible patterns in the deposited material.
The portfolio also records a translucent TPU prototype family. Light reveals the bead structure and the variation of the surfaces across the assembled display.

media.alt: Three white printed objects compare different degrees of twist and bead pattern.
media.caption: The physical geometry-development prototypes.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

media.alt: A group of translucent printed objects is lit from below, revealing their surface patterns.
media.caption: The portfolio identifies this demonstration and prototype family as TPU.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie. Photographer not individually identified.

projects.title: HC3DP Caustics
projects.subtitle: Inflation-based Pattern Exploration
projects.summary: Inflated printed shells and patterned paths shape the light around them.
projects.metadataDescription: A Group-Red study of inflated printed shells, computational paths and photographed caustic light patterns.

hero.alt: Transparent printed shells stand on a table, with light passing through their inflated surfaces.
hero.caption: Physical shells from the Group-Red inflation and caustics study.
hero.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Inflated shells and light.
paragraphs: The team explored complex caustic patterns through simple shell geometries. The initial concept drew on Greek meander motifs and the Hilbert curve.
The source workflow combines a pattern within each layer with planar layer addition.

media.alt: An original diagram pairs the printing tool and inflated shell with three parallel point rows.
media.caption: The original layer-slicing and curve-division diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Paths and frames.
paragraphs: The computational workflow divides layers into bottom, middle and top point rows. Connections between those rows define the path.
The original diagrams show how the team arranged and tilted frames along that path.

media.alt: An original diagram connects points across three rows below the printing-tool model.
media.caption: The original diagram of connections between bottom, middle and top point rows.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

media.alt: An original diagram places tilted coordinate frames along a printing path.
media.caption: The original frame-arrangement diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Printing motion.
paragraphs: The source animation presents the tool, shell geometry and path frames together. It records the fabrication strategy as a simulation.
The project notes describe sensitivity to air pressure and cooling during the physical printing experiments.

media.alt: A source simulation frame shows the printing tool and a row of red path frames.
media.caption: A still from the original fabrication-path animation; this is a simulation.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Observed light patterns.
paragraphs: Photographs document the light patterns produced by different printed geometries. These images record the physical experiments.
The team also documented sticking and overinflation. The curved orange samples show the overinflation behaviour described in the presentation.

media.alt: A translucent printed form creates a radiating light pattern on a wall.
media.caption: A photographed caustic pattern produced during the project experiments.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao. Individual media authors are not separately identified.

media.caption: The source presents this material behaviour as overinflation.

projects.title: Special Assemblies
projects.subtitle: V-Shape Modular Based Aggregation
projects.summary: A collaborative study of reciprocal V-shaped stick modules, directional aggregation and robotic assembly planning.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team study connecting V-shaped stick aggregation with robot trajectories and physical assembly prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
projects.role: Collaborative aggregation and robotic assembly research

hero.alt: A curved assembly of wooden sticks rises from a small base beside a robotic arm.
hero.caption: The assembled prototype beside the robotic arm, documented in the original Group6 record.
hero.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A reciprocal starting point.
paragraphs: The project begins with V-shaped wooden-stick modules inspired by reciprocal structures. Each addition changes the relationships between neighbouring sticks.
Physical prototypes connect this bottom-up geometric study with the conditions of robotic assembly.

media.alt: An early wooden-stick aggregation cantilevers from a small dome-shaped foundation.
media.caption: A physical study of the reciprocal stick aggregation and its foundation.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Photographer not individually identified.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Rules guide the next module.
paragraphs: The VStickModule study groups directional aggregation into four choices: NE, NW, SE and SW.
The documented workflow links geometry, assembly data and ROS/MoveIt planning through JSON, simulation and replanning.

media.alt: Module diagrams and sequential stick assemblies show four directional aggregation choices.
media.caption: The original VStickModule and directional-aggregation diagrams, with their figure captions.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Original portfolio diagram.

media.alt: Workflow diagrams connect module generation, ROS and MoveIt planning, JSON data, simulation and replanning.
media.caption: The original software and JSON-based robotic planning workflow.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Original portfolio diagram.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Plan the assembly sequence.
paragraphs: Pick, place, exit and insert trajectories organise the robot movement around the growing structure.
The team studies stick ordering and tool-frame direction, including a Z-axis correction intended to reduce gripper interference with the table.

media.alt: A robotic assembly diagram labels pick, approach, safe, place and exit frames around the stick prototype.
media.caption: The recorded pick, place, exit and insert trajectory stages for V-stick aggregation.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Original portfolio diagram.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: From modules to a prototype.
paragraphs: The physical assembly records show the accumulated stick relationships from front and top views.
These are experimental prototypes; the source records do not establish exhaustive collision testing or measured fabrication performance.

media.alt: A front view shows the rising wooden-stick assembly under the robot gripper.
media.caption: The physical prototype from a second viewpoint.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Photographer not individually identified.

media.alt: A view from above shows crossing wooden sticks and their repeated contact points beside the robot.
media.caption: A top view of the stick relationships in the assembled prototype.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Photographer not individually identified.
